issues.legal_issue: A lessor may maintain an ejectment action based on forfeiture for rent default under a lease made before the written-notice requirement took effect without first serving written notice of an intention to terminate.
material_facts: The lease was executed before the statutory written-notice requirement took effect and provided that the tenant's rights would end on default in payment of rent.
Rent remained unpaid, and the lessor brought an ejectment suit based on forfeiture without first giving written notice of an intention to terminate the lease.
issues.conclusion: The written-notice requirement did not apply to the lease, and filing the ejectment suit was a sufficient expression of the lessor's intention to rely on the forfeiture. The suit was maintainable without prior written notice.
issues.legal_principle: Transfer of Property Act, 1882, sections 2 and 111(g), as amended by Act XX of 1929, and section 63 of that amending Act: the written-notice amendment was not retrospective and did not apply to transfers made before 1 April 1930. The requirement of written notice was not based on a general principle of justice, equity and good conscience. Under the earlier rule, the lessor had to express an unequivocal intention to take advantage of the breach, and institution of the suit could do so. The Court relied on Toleman v. Portbury, Prakash Chandra Das v. Rajendra Nath Basu, Rama Aiyangar v. Guruswami Chetty and Venkatachari v. Rangaswami Aiyar, and disapproved Umar Pulavar v. Dawood Rowther, Brahmayya v. Sundaramma and Tatya Savla Sudrik v. Yeshwanta Kondiba Mulay.

rule.if: ejectment_proceeding and pre_requirement_lease and rent_defaulted and forfeiture_clause_for_rent_default and landlord_filed_ejectment_action and no_prior_written_notice

predicates.ejectment_proceeding: The proceeding is an ejectment action brought by a lessor against a tenant.
predicates.pre_requirement_lease: The lease was made before the written-notice requirement took effect.
predicates.rent_defaulted: The tenant failed to pay rent when it was due.
predicates.forfeiture_clause_for_rent_default: The lease provided that the tenant's rights would end upon default in paying rent.
predicates.landlord_filed_ejectment_action: The lessor filed an action seeking possession based on the tenant's default.
predicates.no_prior_written_notice: The lessor did not give the tenant written notice of an intention to terminate the lease before filing the action.

issues.definition: When a lessor brings an ejectment action based on rent default under a pre-requirement lease with a rent-default forfeiture clause, and does not first give written notice, the action remains maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: Relief against forfeiture for non-payment of rent is discretionary, and a higher court should not overturn a fact-based refusal absent an improper exercise of that discretion.
material_facts: The tenant repeatedly failed to pay rent for extended periods, and the landlord repeatedly had to bring ejectment suits to recover possession.
Relief against forfeiture had previously been granted to the tenant on several occasions, and the tenant had been warned that further relief might not be granted after another default.

The lower courts found the tenant's conduct contumacious and its defences false, refused relief against forfeiture, and the High Court found no basis to interfere with that exercise of discretion in second appeal.
issues.conclusion: The tenant was not entitled to relief against forfeiture as of right. Given the repeated defaults and the tenant's conduct, the lower courts were justified in refusing relief, and the High Court properly declined to interfere in second appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Transfer of Property Act, 1882, section 114, gives the court discretion to grant relief against forfeiture for non-payment of rent; compliance with the section's payment conditions does not make relief an automatic entitlement. The court should assess each case on its circumstances, including delay, the parties' conduct and the difficulties caused to the landlord. Equitable relief may be refused where the tenant's conduct disentitles it to relief. The Court relied on Appaya Shetty v. Mohammad Beari and Hyman v. Rose, and also referred to Ramakrishna Mallya v. Baburaya and Ramabrahmam v. Rami Reddi. It rejected the contention that relief must be granted unless third-party interests intervene, and distinguished the proposition in Debendralal Khan v. F. M. A. Cohen that would make relief effectively automatic.

rule.if: second_appeal_from_refusal_of_relief and lower_courts_denied_relief and chronic_rent_default and repeated_prior_relief and repeated_false_defenses and discretion_based_on_case_materials

predicates.second_appeal_from_refusal_of_relief: The proceeding is a second appeal challenging the refusal of relief against forfeiture.
predicates.lower_courts_denied_relief: The lower courts refused to grant the tenant relief against forfeiture.
predicates.chronic_rent_default: The tenant repeatedly failed to pay rent on time, with rent remaining unpaid for extended periods.
predicates.repeated_prior_relief: The tenant had previously received relief against forfeiture on several occasions.
predicates.repeated_false_defenses: The tenant repeatedly advanced defences that the courts found false.
predicates.discretion_based_on_case_materials: The lower courts based their decision on relevant evidence about the tenant's delay and conduct and the difficulties caused to the landlord.

issues.definition: When a second appeal challenges a refusal of relief, and that refusal rests on relevant case materials showing repeated default and conduct against a background of prior relief, the relief may be refused and the refusal left undisturbed.
